issues.legal_issue: Long-standing use of a privately owned charitable premises by members of the public does not, without evidence of complete dedication, establish that the premises belong to a public trust.
material_facts: The premises had been used as a place of lodging by travellers and fair visitors for a long period, and some members of the public could stay without charge.
The public’s use was limited: longer stays and use of certain rooms required the owner’s permission, and the premises could also be used for other purposes with permission.
The owners and their predecessors retained control and management, let shops and received the rents, appointed and paid a caretaker, and maintained the premises from their own funds.

Revenue records recorded ownership in the family, while no instrument of dedication, public contribution to maintenance, public participation in management, or public right to use the premises was proved.
The Advocate General brought a suit seeking relief on the basis that the premises had been dedicated as a public trust.
issues.conclusion: The evidence did not establish a complete dedication to the public or the creation of a public trust. Long use as a place of lodging, by itself, was insufficient to establish such a trust.
issues.legal_principle: A Hindu may create a charitable endowment without a written instrument, but there must be clear and unequivocal evidence of an intention to create a trust and a complete dedication that extinguishes the founder’s private ownership. In the absence of an express endowment, the institution’s history and the conduct of the founder and successors determine the character of the dedication. Public use is not enough unless the circumstances support use as of right; retained private control and management, restricted access, and the absence of public contributions are relevant. Revenue entries are presumed correct under Section 35 of the Evidence Act, though that presumption is rebuttable. The Court relied on Menakuru Dasaratharami Reddi v. Duddukuru Subba Rao; Maharani Hemanta Kumari Debi v. Gauri Shankar Tewari; Bihar State Board Religious Trust v. Mahant Sri Biseshwar Das; Babu Bhagwan Din v. Gir Har Saroop; and Sri Radhakanta Deb v. Commissioner of Hindu Religious Endowments.

rule.if: public_trust_suit and owner_retained_control and public_use_restricted and not public_management and not public_maintenance_contributions

predicates.public_trust_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking relief on the basis that property had been dedicated to the public as a trust.
predicates.owner_retained_control: The owner or the owner’s successors controlled the property, managed it, received its income, or maintained it from private funds.
predicates.public_use_restricted: Members of the public could use the property only within limits or with the owner’s permission.
predicates.public_management: Members of the public participated in managing the property or had a role in its administration.
predicates.public_maintenance_contributions: Members of the public contributed to maintaining the property.

issues.definition: When a public-trust suit concerns property whose owner retained control, public use was restricted, and the public neither managed nor contributed to maintaining it, the claimed public trust is not established.

issues.legal_issue: A suit seeking relief under the procedure for public trusts cannot proceed unless the property is shown to be held in a public trust.
material_facts: The suit sought relief on the allegation that the premises had been dedicated to the public as a trust.
The evidence did not establish complete public dedication; the owners retained control and the premises’ use by the public was limited.
The High Court had treated the premises as a public trust and set aside the trial court’s judgment, but the Supreme Court found that conclusion unsustainable.
issues.conclusion: Because a public trust was not established, the suit under Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure could not be maintained on the facts of this case, and the High Court’s judgment could not stand.
issues.legal_principle: Section 92 of the Code of Civil Procedure applies to public trusts, not private trusts. The Court relied on Mahant Ram Saroop Dasji v. S.P. Sahi and Bihar State Board Religious Trust v. Mahant Sri Biseshwar Das, which recognize that Hindu law permits private as well as public trusts and that the statutory provisions in this field apply to public trusts alone.

predicates.public_trust_remedy_suit: A claimant brought a suit seeking the special remedy available for administering or protecting a public trust.
predicates.property_shown_to_be_publicly_dedicated: The evidence showed that the property had been completely dedicated to a public trust.

issues.definition: A suit seeking the special remedy for a public trust is not maintainable when the evidence does not show that the property was completely dedicated to a public trust.
